13250: "Ragtag" describes a group of people — or a collection of things — that is disorganized, randomly thrown together, and made up of mismatched parts that don't really belong with each other. Picture a team hastily assembled from whoever happened to be available, with no planning, no unified look, and no clear structure. That messy, scraped-together quality is exactly what "ragtag" captures.

When you call a group "ragtag," you're saying it looks rough around the edges. The people in it might have different backgrounds, different abilities (or lack of them), and different appearances — with nothing tying them together neatly. There's an underlying sense of low resources, poor preparation, or general untidiness.

A ragtag army, for example, is not a well-drilled, well-equipped military force. It's a band of fighters who grabbed whatever weapons they could find, are wearing mismatched clothing, and have no real chain of command. They look nothing like a proper army.
What kinds of things does it describe?

"Ragtag" almost always sits directly before a noun that refers to a group or collection:

  • A ragtag group of volunteers
  • A ragtag band of rebels
  • A ragtag crew / ragtag team / ragtag army
  • A ragtag collection of old furniture

Notice it works for both people and things. A ragtag collection of tools is a jumbled assortment of mismatched, worn-out items — nothing coordinated, nothing organized.
The tone — mostly negative, but sometimes affectionate

"Ragtag" is a mildly negative word in most situations. It signals that something is unimpressive, unpolished, or assembled without care. If someone calls your team "ragtag," they're implying it looks amateurish and underprepared.

However — and this is an important nuance — "ragtag" can also carry a warm, even admiring tone, especially in storytelling. Think of the classic underdog story: a ragtag group of misfits who shouldn't work together, and yet, against all odds, they come through and win. Here, "ragtag" isn't pure criticism. It acknowledges the messiness while quietly celebrating the scrappy, unlikely spirit of the group. The word hints at a story: these people don't look like winners on paper — and that's precisely what makes their victory interesting.

So context is everything. The same word can be dismissive in one sentence and almost endearing in another.
Example sentences — feel how it works

• "The general looked at his ragtag army with a sigh — half of them didn't even have proper boots." → clear negative use; the army is pitiful and underprepared.
  • "A ragtag bunch of neighborhood kids formed a band and ended up playing at the city festival." → affectionate and slightly admiring; their messiness is part of their charm.
  • "The detective's office was filled with a ragtag collection of case files, old coffee cups, and broken pens." → used for objects; conveys a cluttered, disorganized environment.

In each case, "ragtag" immediately paints a picture of disorder, mismatch, and rough edges.
How it differs from similar words

Motley is the closest relative — as in "a motley crew." Both words suggest a mismatched, oddly assorted group. But "motley" puts emphasis on striking variety and contrast between members — the colorful, eccentric differences. "Ragtag" adds something extra: a sense of disorder, low quality, and scrappiness. A motley crew might feel vibrant and eccentric; a ragtag bunch feels like it was barely scraped together from the leftovers.

Makeshift means hastily assembled from whatever is available, but it applies mostly to objects or plans — a makeshift shelter, a makeshift solution — and doesn't carry the sense of internal mismatch that "ragtag" does.

Disorganized is plain and neutral — it states a fact. "Ragtag" is far more vivid and opinionated — it paints a picture and carries a judgment.

"Ragtag" almost always appears directly before the noun it describes — this is called an attributive position. You naturally say "a ragtag group" rather than "the group is ragtag". The second version is technically possible, but the first is how native speakers almost always use it.
The one-line summary to remember it forever:
"Ragtag" = randomly thrown together, mismatched, and disorganized — looking like it barely came together at all.
13251:
A rail is a long, rigid bar — usually made of wood or metal — that is fixed in place to support, guide, separate, or protect. That's the central image: a bar that runs along something, doing a job.

Almost every meaning of "rail" as a noun grows from this image.
1. A bar for support and safety

The most everyday meaning: a rail is a bar you hold onto or lean against so you don't fall. You see these everywhere:

  • The bar running along a staircase that you grip as you climb — a handrail
  • The barrier of bars around a balcony, bridge, or rooftop — a railing (a series of rails held up by posts)
  • The bars you grab inside a bus or subway car when you're standing

The job of a rail in this sense is simple: keep people safe and steady.
2. A bar that forms a fence or boundary

A rail also refers to a horizontal bar in a fence. A typical wooden fence has vertical posts hammered into the ground, and horizontal bars — the rails — running between them. A classic "split-rail fence" (common in old American farms) is made of long, split pieces of wood laid across posts as rails.

In horse racing, "the rail" is the fence running along the inside edge of the racetrack. A jockey who keeps their horse close to this boundary is racing "on the rail" — a shorter path, and often an advantage.
3. The tracks that trains run on — and train travel itself

Two long, parallel strips of steel laid on the ground that trains roll along — these are called rails. One rail for the left wheels, one for the right. Together they make up a railway track (or "railroad track" in American English). The rails are thick, heavy steel bars, because they must carry the enormous weight of entire trains, thousands of times a day.

From this, "rail" grew to mean the entire system of train travel:

  • "We crossed the country by rail." — by train
  • "The rail network" — all the train lines in a region or country
  • "Rail traffic" — trains moving through the system
  • "Rail strike" — a stoppage of train services

The third rail deserves special mention. Most train tracks have just two rails. But in many metro (subway) systems, there's a third rail running beside the other two. This rail carries high-voltage electricity that powers the trains. Touching it is instantly fatal. Because of this danger, "the third rail" has entered everyday language as a metaphor for any topic so explosive or controversial that people are afraid to go near it — especially in politics. "Pension reform is the third rail of that election — nobody wants to touch it."
4. The horizontal piece in a door or cabinet frame

In carpentry and furniture-making, rail has a precise meaning: it's the horizontal member in a rectangular frame. A wooden door, for example, is built like a picture frame — vertical pieces run up the sides (called stiles) and horizontal pieces run across the top, bottom, and middle (called rails). The top rail, bottom rail, and sometimes a mid rail hold the door together and give it structure. Cabinet doors, wooden panels, and window frames are built the same way. This sense is specific to woodworking and construction.

On a boat or ship, the rail is the bar or ridge running along the very top of the side of the vessel — the edge where the side of the ship meets open air. It's the part you lean on when you look out to sea. When cargo or a person goes "over the rail," it means they've fallen off the side of the ship. The rail at the very back (stern) of a ship has its own name: the taffrail.

In surfing, the rails are the two long side edges of a surfboard — where the flat top surface curves down to meet the bottom. Every surfboard has a left rail and a right rail. The shape of these edges — how sharp, how rounded, how thick — has a big effect on how the board responds in water. This is very much a technical term used by surfers and board-shapers.

Completely separate from all the bar/track meanings, a rail is also a type of bird. Rails are a large family of birds (Rallidae) that live mostly in wetlands, marshes, and thick grasses. They are famously secretive and hard to spot — they stay hidden deep in vegetation and are much more often heard than seen. Their calls can be loud and distinctive, but the birds themselves are elusive.

Well-known examples include the water rail, the corncrake, and the sora. Rails are generally slender-bodied (they need to squeeze through dense reeds), with strong legs and short wings. Many are poor fliers despite having wings. The expression "thin as a rail" — meaning very skinny — is believed by some to refer to these slim birds, though others think it refers to the thinness of a wooden fence rail.

Most of these come from the train-track meaning:

  • "Off the rails" — Out of control; behaving erratically or destructively. A train that literally leaves the rails is dangerous and going nowhere. Figuratively: "After the scandal, his career went completely off the rails."
  • "Back on the rails" — Returning to normal functioning after a period of chaos or trouble.
  • "By rail" — By train. "The goods are transported by rail."
  • "Guardrail" — A strong protective rail along the side of a road, highway, bridge, or staircase, designed to stop vehicles or people from going over the edge.
  • "Handrail" — The rail you hold with your hand on stairs, ramps, or escalators.
  • "Third rail" (figurative) — A subject so politically or socially dangerous that people avoid it. "Healthcare costs are the third rail no politician wants to touch."

If you look at almost every meaning of "rail" (except the bird), you'll find the same underlying image: a long, firm bar or strip that runs along the length of something. It runs along your staircase (handrail). It runs along the ground for trains (railway rail). It runs horizontally in a fence or a door frame. It runs along the top edge of a ship's side. It runs along the sides of a surfboard.

The word is really just describing that shape and function — a long, rigid bar in place along something — applied to many different contexts. Once you see that core image, the meanings stop feeling like a random list and start feeling like variations on a single idea.

The bird called a rail is the one exception — that's a separate word that happens to be spelled the same way, and has nothing to do with bars or tracks.
13252:
To rail means to complain or protest in a loud, angry, and bitter way — especially about something you feel is deeply unfair or wrong.

It is not ordinary complaining. When someone rails, they are expressing strong, heated frustration — often passionately and at length. Think of it as the verbal equivalent of a storm: forceful, sharp, and hard to ignore.

1. Rail against something

This is the most common usage. You rail against a thing — a system, a rule, an idea, an injustice.

She railed against the new law that cut workers' wages.

The protesters railed against government corruption.

He spent years railing against the unfairness of the education system.

Here, the target of the anger is usually something abstract or systemic — a policy, a decision, a situation, an institution.

2. Rail at someone or something

Here, the anger is directed more personally — at a person, a group, or even a thing you're treating as if it can hear you.

The coach railed at his players for their lack of effort.

She railed at the slow internet connection in frustration.

He railed at his doctor for not taking his symptoms seriously.

This is important: railing is emotional, not rational. When someone rails, they are not calmly arguing a point or politely raising a concern. They are venting. The tone is heated. The language is strong. The frustration has boiled over.

It also carries a subtle implication that the railing may not actually change anything. You can rail all you want, but the situation might stay the same. This gives the word a slightly helpless quality alongside its anger — like someone shouting into the wind.

Compare these sentences:

  • He argued against the decision. → calm, measured, logical
  • He complained about the decision. → mild, ordinary
  • He railed against the decision. → furious, passionate, intense — perhaps even a little desperate

The word is used in a wide variety of contexts:

  • A politician rails against a rival's policies.
  • A writer rails against censorship in their books.
  • A parent rails at a child who keeps repeating the same mistake.
  • A patient rails against a broken healthcare system.
  • A character in a novel rails at the cruelty of fate.

It is a word you will often see in writing, journalism, and literature — slightly more formal than everyday speech, but not rare.

"Rail" as a verb also has a separate, more literal meaning: to enclose or fence off an area using rails (the physical bars or posts used in fencing).

The workers railed off the construction site to keep people away.

The garden was railed in to protect it from animals.

This usage is straightforward — you are simply building or using a barrier made of rails. You will mostly encounter this in descriptions of physical spaces, construction, or historical writing. It is far less common than the "angry protest" meaning above.

Primary meaningTo complain or protest loudly, bitterly, and angrily — especially about something felt to be unjust
Rail againstDirected at a system, idea, or situation
Rail atDirected at a person or group
ToneEmotional, heated, forceful — not calm
Secondary meaningTo fence or enclose an area with rails
One Final Example to Tie It Together

Imagine a man who has just been unfairly fired from his job. He storms out of the office and spends the next hour shouting about how corrupt the company is, how the boss has always been biased against him, and how the whole system is rigged. He is not problem-solving. He is not being diplomatic. He is just furious.

That man is railing — and now you know exactly what that means.
13253:
A railing is a barrier or fence-like structure made of one or more horizontal bars — called rails — that are held up by vertical posts. Its job is to run along the edge of something elevated or hazardous, giving people a structure to hold onto or to stop them from falling.

You have almost certainly seen railings everywhere: on staircases, balconies, bridges, ramps, and terraces.

Picture a typical staircase. As you climb up, there is a long bar running alongside it at roughly hand height — that is the rail. It is held up by a row of vertical posts rising from the steps. Together, the whole structure — the bar plus the posts — is called the railing.

Railings can be made of:

  • Metal — iron, steel, or aluminum (very common, especially outdoors)
  • Wood — common on indoor staircases and porches
  • Glass — modern buildings sometimes use glass panels as railings for an open look
  • Plastic or PVC — lighter, cheaper option

They can be plain and functional, or highly decorative with intricate patterns worked into the metal or wood.

A railing serves three distinct purposes:

1. Safety — preventing falls
This is its most important job. On a balcony, bridge, rooftop, or any elevated surface, a railing acts as a physical barrier. It stops people from accidentally stepping off the edge and falling. Building codes in most countries legally require railings anywhere there is a significant drop.

2. Support — something to grip
On a staircase or ramp, the railing gives you something to hold onto as you move. This helps with balance, especially for elderly people, children, or anyone carrying something heavy. On an escalator, the moving rubber handrail at the sides is a kind of railing too.

3. Boundary — marking off a space
Sometimes a railing signals "do not cross this line" without necessarily being about a fall risk. Think of the low railing that separates the crowd from a stage at a concert, or the railing that marks the boundary of a restricted zone at an airport or museum.

Railings appear almost anywhere people move around elevated or hazardous spaces:

  • Along the sides of staircases — indoors and outdoors
  • On balconies and terraces — to keep people from falling off
  • Along bridges and overpasses — on both sides for safety
  • On porches and decks of houses
  • Around the edges of flat rooftops
  • Along train and metro platforms — sometimes as a partial barrier
  • Around swimming pools, pits, or open drops — wherever a fall would be dangerous
  • Along wheelchair ramps — to give support on the incline

When used in the plural — railings — the word can specifically mean a fence made of a series of vertical metal bars, often with pointed or decorative tops, that encloses or surrounds an area like a garden, park, or the front of a building. This usage is especially common in British English.

"The children pressed their faces against the iron railings of the park."

Here, "railings" refers to the iron fence of vertical bars running around the park's perimeter — not a handrail on a staircase, but a fence-type structure made in the same general way.
The second, separate meaning: angry complaints

"Railing" (and its plural, "railings") has an entirely different second meaning that has nothing to do with physical structures. It can refer to bitter, angry protests, rants, or criticisms directed at someone or something.

This comes from the verb to rail, which means to speak or shout angrily and at length against something.

"His railings against the new policy went on for hours."
"The crowd grew tired of the politician's endless railing."

In these examples, "railings" and "railing" mean prolonged, angry complaints or verbal attacks — not a physical barrier. You will encounter this sense more often in books, journalism, and formal writing than in casual speech.
A quick summary to lock it in

SituationWhat "railing" means
  • "Hold the railing as you go down the stairs" → the bar on the side of the staircase you grip for support
  • "The balcony had a wrought-iron railing" → the decorative metal barrier along the balcony's edge
  • "The park was enclosed by iron railings" → a fence of vertical metal bars surrounding the park
  • "Her railings against her boss were exhausting" → her angry, repeated complaints

The primary and most common meaning of "railing" is the physical barrier — a structure of rails and posts that runs along edges, stairs, and balconies for safety and support. The secondary meaning (angry complaints) is real but far less common, and context will always make it obvious which one is meant: if someone is talking about a building, staircase, or outdoor space, it is the physical structure; if someone is talking about a person's speech or behavior, it is the angry complaints.
13254:
Raillery is good-natured, playful teasing — the kind where everyone laughs, including the person being teased.

Imagine two close friends. One of them always shows up five minutes late to everything. The other constantly jokes about it — "Oh look, he actually found a clock!" — and the late friend laughs and fires back something equally witty. That back-and-forth? That's raillery. It's light, it's clever, and most importantly, it carries no real venom. The goal is amusement, not embarrassment.

Raillery lives in a very specific emotional zone. It's warmer than sarcasm, gentler than mockery, sharper than plain flattery, and wittier than simple chitchat. It sits right at the sweet spot where humor and affection meet. There's always a faint sting — that's what makes it funny — but the sting is never deep enough to wound. Think of it like a playful nudge on the arm, not a punch.

It's also often mutual. Raillery tends to go both ways. It's the kind of teasing that invites a clever comeback, rather than silence or hurt feelings. This is why it feels more like sport than attack. A good raillery exchange crackles with wit, and both sides are expected to give as good as they get.

It's not sarcasm, which can be cold and cutting. It's not satire, which has a serious social or political purpose. It's not bullying, which is aimed at humiliating someone. And it's not simple flattery or empty small talk. Raillery has a playful bite — that's what separates it from mere politeness — but that bite is always wrapped in warmth.

The tone of the word itself is somewhat literary and refined. You won't often hear it in casual everyday conversation today. You're more likely to encounter it in older literature, formal writing, or when someone wants to describe a particularly witty, sophisticated kind of banter. When an author writes that two characters engaged in raillery, they're painting a scene of intelligent, cheerful verbal sparring — the kind you might picture in a drawing room, between sharp-minded people who genuinely enjoy each other.

A simple way to remember it: If teasing were on a scale from "warm hug" to "cold slap," raillery would be a friendly, laughing shove. Affectionate. Intentionally witty. Harmless by design.
13255: The simple truth: Raiment means clothing or garments. That's its core meaning. But there is much more to understand about how this word works and when it's used, which is what separates knowing a word from truly understanding it.
It's not just any word for "clothes"

English has many words for clothing — clothes, garments, apparel, attire, dress, garb. Raiment belongs to this family, but it occupies a special, elevated corner of it.

Raiment is a literary and poetic word. It is old-fashioned in the sense that ordinary people don't use it in daily conversation. You would never hear someone say, "I left my raiment on the floor." That would sound bizarre. Instead, you encounter raiment in the Bible, in poetry, in old literature, in fantasy writing, and in formal or ceremonial prose — anywhere that language is meant to feel grand, majestic, or beautiful.

Think of it this way: "clothes" is what you say. "Raiment" is what a narrator says when describing a king, an angel, or a bride in a way that makes the moment feel weighty and significant.
What it suggests, not just what it means

Raiment doesn't just mean clothing — it tends to carry a feeling of beauty, splendor, or importance about the clothing being described. When a writer chooses the word raiment over dress or garments, they are silently signaling that these clothes are worth noticing. They might be rich, flowing, white, golden, ceremonial, or simply described with reverence.

This is why raiment appears so often in scripture and in scenes involving royalty or divine figures. The word elevates the subject.

That said, raiment doesn't strictly require that the clothing be fine or expensive. Technically, it just means clothing. But in practice, writers reach for this word when there's something worth admiring about the garments in question — or when the writing itself is supposed to feel elevated, even if the clothes are simple.

Raiment is an uncountable noun, which means it works exactly like the word "clothing" — not like the word "shirt."

You do not say:

  • "a raiment"
  • "two raiments"
  • "many raiments"

You say:

  • "his raiment"
  • "white raiment"
  • "raiment of silk and gold"

Just as you'd say "her clothing was torn" and not "her clothings were torn," you say "his raiment was torn" — treating it as a single collective idea, not individual countable pieces.

Here are some examples that show how the word actually lives in a sentence:

"And why take ye thought for raiment?" — This is from the Bible (Matthew 6:28, King James Version), where Jesus asks why people worry about what they will wear. The use of raiment gives the line its solemn, scriptural weight.

"The angel stood before them, clothed in raiment white as snow." — Here raiment evokes purity and divine majesty. The word choice alone makes the scene feel otherworldly.

"The old king lay in a simple bed, stripped of his raiment and his power." — Even in a scene of loss and plainness, the word raiment reminds you that this man once wore robes of authority.

"She prepared her wedding raiment with great care." — Here raiment simply means a wedding dress and its accompanying garments, but calling it raiment makes the preparation feel ceremonial and meaningful.
How it compares to similar words

Since you'll encounter these words together in reading, here's how raiment sits among its closest relatives:

Clothes / Clothing — The neutral, everyday term. No special feeling attached. This is what you use in normal life.

Garments — Slightly more formal than clothes, but still fairly neutral. Often used in practical or commercial contexts (the garment industry, for instance).

Apparel — More formal than clothes, but modern. Used in business and fashion (sports apparel, outdoor apparel).

Attire — Formal and dignified, often used for specific occasions ("formal attire," "business attire"). More modern than raiment.

Raiment — The most literary, archaic, and poetic of all. Carries the most sense of grandeur. Belongs in scripture, old texts, poetry, and fantasy.

Vestments — Specifically refers to ceremonial clothing worn by clergy or religious figures. Narrower than raiment.

You are most likely to see raiment in:

The Bible (especially the King James Version, which uses it frequently). Shakespeare and other old English literature. Fantasy and epic fiction, where authors deliberately reach for archaic language to create a sense of another world or ancient time. Poetry, particularly from earlier centuries. Formal ceremonial writing, such as passages describing coronations, weddings, or funerals in literary contexts.

You are very unlikely to see it in news articles, casual writing, or modern everyday prose — unless someone is being deliberately poetic or playful.
The one-sentence definition, now with full meaning behind it

Raiment means clothing or garments — used as a literary, poetic, and archaic word that lends a sense of grandeur, beauty, or solemnity to the garments being described, and found almost exclusively in elevated writing such as scripture, old literature, poetry, and fantasy.

Now when you encounter this word anywhere, you'll know exactly what it means, what it feels like, and why the writer chose it.
13256:
"It's raining cats and dogs" means it is raining very heavily — not just a light shower or drizzle, but a powerful, intense downpour where water is falling fast and hard.

It does not literally mean animals are falling from the sky. No cats or dogs are involved at all. It is a figurative expression — a colourful, exaggerated way of describing extremely heavy rainfall.

Think of it this way: when you say "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse," you don't mean you'll actually eat a horse. You just mean you're very hungry. "Raining cats and dogs" works the same way — you're saying it's very, very rainy.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are some natural examples:

  • "Take an umbrella — it's raining cats and dogs outside!"
  • "The match was cancelled because it was raining cats and dogs all afternoon."
  • "We couldn't go for a walk. It rained cats and dogs the whole day."
  • "I got completely soaked walking to the bus stop. It was raining cats and dogs!"

Notice that you almost always say "raining cats and dogs" — not "falling cats and dogs" or "pouring cats and dogs." The word "raining" stays fixed in the phrase.
Origin — Where Did This Strange Phrase Come From?

This is one of the most debated idioms in the English language, and no one knows for certain where it comes from. But here are the most widely accepted and interesting theories:

Theory 1: The Streets of Old England (Most Popular Theory)

In 17th and 18th century England, cities like London had no proper drainage or sewage systems. Dead animals — stray cats and dogs — often lay in the streets or on rooftops. When it rained heavily, flash floods would wash these carcasses through the streets. So after a violent rainstorm, people would literally see cats and dogs lying in the streets, as if they had fallen from the sky. The expression may have grown out of this shocking sight.

Theory 2: Norse Mythology

In ancient Norse (Scandinavian) mythology, cats were associated with rain and storms, while dogs were associated with wind. Odin, the Norse god, was often depicted with wolves (similar to dogs). So "raining cats and dogs" may have been a poetic way of saying "a storm of rain and wind" — combining the two symbols.

Theory 3: The Greek Expression

An old Greek expression, "cata doxa," means "contrary to experience" or "unbelievably hard." Some believe English speakers transformed this into "cats and dogs" over time as a way of saying the rain was unbelievably heavy. However, this theory is the least supported by language historians.

The Earliest Written Use

The earliest known printed use of this phrase appears in Jonathan Swift's 1738 work A Complete Collection of Genteel and Ingenious Conversation, where he wrote something very close to the modern phrase. An even earlier use appears in 1651, in a poem by English playwright Henry Vaughan, who described a roof as secure against "dogs and cats rained in shower."

This tells us the phrase has been around for at least 375 years.
Why English Uses Such Strange Imagery

English is full of idioms that use exaggerated or impossible imagery to express intensity. "Raining cats and dogs" belongs to a family of expressions where something impossible or absurd is described to emphasise how extreme a situation is. The very strangeness of the image — animals falling from the sky — is what makes it memorable and powerful. It immediately signals to the listener: this is not ordinary rain.
Register — When and Where to Use It

"Raining cats and dogs" is an informal expression. This means:

Use it freely in:

  • Casual conversations with friends and family
  • Informal writing (text messages, personal emails, social media)
  • Storytelling

Avoid it in:

  • Formal reports, academic essays, or business emails
  • Weather forecasts or scientific writing
  • Professional or official communication

In formal writing, you would simply say: "Heavy rainfall was recorded throughout the afternoon" or "There was a severe downpour."

In English, there are other ways to describe the same thing:

  • "It's pouring" — short and common
  • "It's bucketing down" — used more in British English
  • "It's coming down in sheets" — describes rain falling in wide, sweeping waves
  • "It's a deluge" — more formal; a deluge is a biblical-scale flood

Other languages also have their own colourful equivalents:

  • In French: "Il pleut des cordes" — "It's raining ropes"
  • In German: "Es regnet Bindfäden" — "It's raining twine/string"
  • In Greek: "Βρέχει καρεκλοπόδαρα" — "It's raining chair legs"

This shows that many cultures use vivid, impossible images to describe heavy rain — English is not alone!

• ❌ Don't say: "It rained cats and dogs of water." — Incorrect; don't add extra words.
  • ❌ Don't say: "It's pouring cats and dogs." — Incorrect; always use "raining," not "pouring."
  • ❌ Don't use it for light rain. If it's just drizzling, this phrase would be an exaggeration too far and would sound wrong.
  • ✅ Do say: "It was raining cats and dogs" (past), "It is raining cats and dogs" (present), "It will probably rain cats and dogs tomorrow" (future).

MeaningRaining very heavily
TypeInformal idiom / figurative expression
Literal?No — no animals involved
OriginLikely 17th century England; exact origin debated
First recorded useAround 1651
Always paired withThe word "raining"
Use inCasual speech and informal writing

That's everything you need to know about "raining cats and dogs" — its meaning, history, correct usage, variations, and pitfalls, all in one place.
13257:
A rainforest is a thick, dense forest that receives a very large amount of rainfall throughout the year — typically at least 2,000 millimetres (about 79 inches) annually, though many get far more. Because of all this rain and warmth, these forests grow incredibly lush and full, packed with an enormous variety of plants and animals. It is one of the most biologically rich places on Earth.

Think of it this way: a regular forest gets some rain, some sunshine, some dry spells. A rainforest almost never truly dries out. The moisture is constant, and that changes everything about how life grows there.

Not all rainforests are the same. There are two main kinds:

1. Tropical Rainforests
These are the ones most people picture. They sit near the equator — the imaginary belt around the middle of the Earth — where the sun shines intensely and temperatures stay hot (usually between 24°C and 30°C) all year round. There is no real "winter." Rain falls heavily and frequently. The Amazon in South America, the Congo Basin in Africa, and the rainforests of Southeast Asia (like in Borneo and Sumatra) are all tropical rainforests.

2. Temperate Rainforests
These grow farther from the equator, in cooler regions, but still receive enormous amounts of rain. They are much rarer than tropical rainforests. You find them along certain coastlines where ocean winds bring heavy moisture — such as in the Pacific Northwest of North America (parts of the U.S. state of Washington and Canada's British Columbia), southern Chile, and parts of New Zealand. These forests are cool, misty, and ancient-feeling, filled with giant mossy trees.

When people say "rainforest" without any extra word before it, they almost always mean a tropical rainforest.
What a Rainforest Actually Looks Like

A rainforest is not just "a lot of trees." It is a complex, layered world, almost like a multi-storey building made entirely of living things.

The Emergent Layer — This is the very top. A few exceptionally tall trees burst above everything else, sometimes reaching 60 metres (about 200 feet) or more. Their crowns are exposed to full sunlight and strong wind. Eagles, certain butterflies, and other creatures live up here.

The Canopy — Just below the emergents, this is the "roof" of the rainforest. It is a dense, continuous ceiling of leaves and branches, usually 30 to 45 metres high. This layer blocks most of the sunlight from reaching below. Monkeys, sloths, toucans, parrots, and countless insects call this home. The canopy is so thick that rain actually takes several minutes to drip down through it to the ground.

The Understory — Below the canopy is a shadowy, dimmer world. Shorter trees, shrubs, and younger plants grow here, adapted to surviving in low light. Jaguars, frogs, snakes, and many insects live in this layer. The air here is still and humid.

The Forest Floor — At the very bottom, almost no sunlight reaches. It is dark, damp, and warm. Dead leaves, fallen trees, and animal droppings decompose very quickly because of the heat and moisture — this decay feeds the soil and cycles nutrients back into the forest. Large animals like gorillas, tapirs, and many insects live here. The forest floor is not covered with thick grass as many imagine — it is mostly bare, soft earth and leaf litter, because no sunlight reaches to grow much.

1. Extraordinary Biodiversity
Rainforests cover only about 6–7% of the Earth's land surface, yet they are home to more than half of the world's plant and animal species. The Amazon alone holds about 10% of all species on Earth. Millions of species of insects, birds, reptiles, amphibians, mammals, and plants — many not yet even discovered or named by scientists — live in rainforests. This makes them irreplaceable storehouses of life.

2. The Lungs of the Earth
Rainforests absorb massive amounts of carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas) from the atmosphere and release oxygen in return, through the process of photosynthesis. The Amazon rainforest alone produces about 20% of the world's oxygen. This is why they are often called the "lungs of the Earth." They play a critical role in keeping our planet's air breathable and in slowing down climate change.

3. Regulating Weather and Water
Rainforests create their own weather. The trees release enormous amounts of water vapour into the air, which forms clouds and eventually falls as rain — sometimes not just locally, but carried by winds to feed rivers and agriculture hundreds or thousands of kilometres away. Destroying rainforests can disrupt rainfall patterns across entire continents.

4. Medicine and Science
A remarkable share of modern medicines come from rainforest plants — including treatments for cancer, malaria, and heart disease. Scientists believe there are thousands of undiscovered plants and organisms in rainforests that could hold cures for diseases we cannot yet treat. Once a species goes extinct, that potential is lost forever.

5. Home to Indigenous Peoples
Hundreds of indigenous communities have lived in and with rainforests for thousands of years. These peoples have deep, sophisticated knowledge of the forest — its plants, animals, medicines, and ecology.

Rainforests are under serious threat, primarily from human activity.

Deforestation is the biggest danger. Forests are cleared — often by burning — to create farmland (especially for cattle ranching and crops like soy and palm oil), for logging (to sell the timber), and for building roads, mines, and cities. Once a rainforest is cut down, the soil — which is actually quite thin and poor in nutrients, because the nutrients are all locked in the living plants — is quickly washed away by rain. The land often becomes dry and barren. Regrowing a true rainforest, with all its complexity, takes centuries.

Climate change also threatens rainforests. Rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns can push parts of the Amazon, for example, past a "tipping point" where a section of the forest can no longer sustain itself and collapses into a dry savannah-like landscape — a transformation called "dieback."

"Rainforest" is used as a noun, both as a countable noun ("a rainforest," "the rainforests of the world") and in a more general, collective sense ("rainforest destruction," "rainforest conservation"). It can also work as an adjective-modifier before another noun, describing things that belong to or come from such forests — for example, "rainforest species," "rainforest canopy," "rainforest medicine."

Example sentences:

  • "The Amazon is the largest rainforest on Earth."
  • "Many scientists travel to the rainforest to study undiscovered species."
  • "Deforestation is destroying the rainforest at an alarming rate."
  • "The rainforest canopy is so dense that very little sunlight reaches the ground."
  • "She dedicated her life to rainforest conservation."

A rainforest is a dense, wet, biologically extraordinary forest — a place where relentless rain, heat (or cool moisture in temperate types), and the sheer abundance of life create an ecosystem unlike any other on the planet. It is both one of nature's greatest masterpieces and one of its most fragile — irreplaceable, teeming with millions of species, and absolutely vital to the health of the entire Earth.
13258:
"Raise" always means you are causing something to go higher, increase, or come into being. You are the one doing it. Something else is receiving your action.

This is the soul of the word. Every meaning of "raise" you will ever encounter is a version of this idea — either literally (physically lifting) or figuratively (causing something to grow, intensify, or appear).
One Grammar Rule You Must Know

"Raise" always needs an object — meaning, you always raise something. You cannot just "raise." You raise your hand. You raise prices. You raise a child.

This is what separates "raise" from "rise." "Rise" happens on its own — the sun rises, prices rise. But with "raise," you are the cause. You are doing it to something.

Think of it this way:

  • The bread rises on its own. → No one is causing it.
  • The baker raises the temperature. → The baker is causing the change.

Keep this rule in mind as you read the rest of this guide.
All the Meanings, One by One

1. To Move Something Physically Upward

This is the most literal meaning. You lift something from a lower position to a higher one.

  • She raised the window blind to let in sunlight.
  • He raised his arm to ask a question in class.
  • The workers raised the flag on the pole.
  • The crane raised the heavy steel beam.

Anything you physically lift or pull upward — you "raise" it.

2. To Increase an Amount, Level, or Degree

Here, "raise" means to make something greater — a number, a price, a temperature, a standard.

  • The company raised the employees' salaries.
  • The government raised taxes this year.
  • He turned the dial to raise the volume.
  • The teacher raised her expectations for the class.
  • Scientists raised the temperature in the experiment.

Notice how in all these cases, something goes up — not in space, but in value or intensity.

3. To Bring Up and Nurture a Child, Animal, or Crop

When you raise a living thing, you take care of it from an early stage of life and help it grow to maturity.

  • Her grandparents raised her after her parents passed away.
  • They raise chickens and goats on their farm.
  • Farmers in this region raise wheat and rice.
  • He was raised in a small village in the mountains. (This means he grew up there, under someone's care.)

Notice that you can "raise" children, animals, and even plants/crops. In all cases, the idea is the same: you are responsible for their growth and survival over a long period.

4. To Bring Up a Topic, Question, or Issue in a Conversation

When you "raise" something in conversation, you bring it to people's attention — you introduce it for others to notice or discuss.

  • She raised an important question during the meeting.
  • Nobody raised any objections to the plan.
  • He raised his concerns about the safety of the building.
  • The journalist raised the issue of corruption.
  • The report raised doubts about the company's honesty.

Think of it as lifting a topic up into the conversation — making it visible, just like lifting something off the floor so everyone can see it.

5. To Collect or Gather Money, Support, or People

When you raise funds, an army, or support, you are gathering resources — bringing them together from different places so that the total grows.

  • The charity raised five million rupees for flood victims.
  • The startup raised funds from investors.
  • The king raised an army to defend the kingdom.
  • They raised enough support to win the election.

The idea is the same — you are causing a number or a group to grow and increase.

6. To Cause a Feeling, Reaction, or Situation to Appear

"Raise" can also mean to produce or trigger something — often a feeling, a reaction, or a situation that wasn't there before.

  • The news raised everyone's hopes.
  • The horror movie raised her anxiety.
  • His rude comment raised eyebrows in the room. (This means people were surprised or disapproving.)
  • The politician's speech raised the crowd's spirits.
  • Her unusual behavior raised suspicion among her colleagues.

Here, you are not lifting a physical thing. You are causing something — a feeling or a reaction — to come into existence or to intensify.

7. To Make Your Voice Louder

When you raise your voice, you speak more loudly. Often this implies anger or urgency, though not always.

  • Please do not raise your voice at me.
  • She had to raise her voice to be heard over the noise.
  • He never raises his voice, even when he's frustrated.

8. To Bring Up Something to a Higher Level or Status

"Raise" can mean to promote, elevate, or upgrade something — in rank, status, importance, or quality.

  • The company raised him to the position of manager.
  • The government plans to raise the standard of public schools.
  • This discovery raised the profile of the young scientist.

9. To Formally End a Restriction or Siege

In formal or official language, "raise" can mean to lift a ban, a blockade, a siege, or sanctions — meaning to end or remove them.

  • The government raised the ban on imports.
  • After months, the army finally raised the siege of the city.
  • The UN voted to raise the sanctions on the country.

Here, "raise" means to "lift" a restriction — as if removing something that was weighing something else down.

10. Specific Uses You Will Encounter

In card games (like poker):
To raise means to increase the bet above what the previous player put in.

  • He raised the bet to a thousand rupees.

To raise a toast:
When people lift their glasses before drinking to honor someone, this is called raising a toast.

  • He raised a toast to the bride and groom.

To raise the alarm:
To alert people about a danger or problem.

  • She raised the alarm when she smelled smoke in the building.

In mathematics:
To raise a number to a power means to multiply it by itself that many times.

  • Two raised to the power of three equals eight. (2³ = 8)

To raise the dead (literary/religious):
To bring someone back to life. Also used figuratively to mean reviving something that had ended or died out.

  • The story says the prophet could raise the dead.
  • She raised the old tradition from obscurity.

These are fixed expressions you will hear very often. Knowing them will save you a lot of confusion.

  • Raise the bar — to set a higher standard for quality or performance.
    "Their new product really raised the bar for the industry."
  • Raise hell / raise a ruckus — to cause trouble, argue loudly, or protest.
    "He raised hell when his order was wrong."
  • Raise the stakes — to make something more important, risky, or competitive.
    "Investing your savings really raises the stakes."
  • Raise awareness — to make people more conscious of an issue.
    "The campaign was designed to raise awareness about mental health."
  • Raise a red flag — to signal a warning or concern.
    "The missing documents raised a red flag for the auditors."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

You almost never need to guess. The word that comes after "raise" tells you everything:

  • Raise + hand/flag/arm/curtain → physical upward movement
  • Raise + salary/price/tax/temperature → increase in amount
  • Raise + child/animals/crops → nurturing and growing
  • Raise + question/issue/concern/objection → bringing something into discussion
  • Raise + money/funds/army → gathering resources
  • Raise + hopes/spirits/doubts/suspicion → causing a feeling or reaction
  • Raise + voice → speaking more loudly
  • Raise + ban/siege/sanctions → formally ending a restriction

Every single meaning of "raise" — whether you're lifting a box, increasing a price, nurturing a child, or starting a conversation about a problem — is a variation of the same idea:

You are causing something to go up, grow, increase, or come into existence.

You are always the agent. You are always the cause. And something else is always moving upward or becoming more because of you.

Master this central idea, and every use of "raise" — even ones you encounter for the first time — will make perfect sense.
13259: The word rake as a noun has four distinct and completely unrelated meanings, each belonging to a different world. Here is every meaning explained fully — with context, examples, and nuance.

This is the most common, everyday meaning.

A rake is a long-handled tool used in gardening and yard work. Picture a long stick (the handle) with a straight bar across the bottom, from which several pointed tines — short teeth — stick outward, like the teeth of a wide comb laid flat.

To use one, you hold the handle upright and drag or push the tined end along the ground.

What it's used for:

  • Gathering fallen leaves — The most iconic use. In autumn, people rake leaves into piles to bag or compost them.
  • Breaking up and leveling soil — After digging a garden bed, you drag a rake across the surface to crush hard clumps of earth and make it flat and even before planting.
  • Clearing debris — Removing stones, twigs, and dead grass from a lawn or garden bed.
  • Spreading material — Distributing mulch, compost, or gravel evenly across a surface.

The two main types:

There are two very different rakes built for different jobs:

Leaf rake (fan rake): Has many thin, flexible tines fanned out in a wide shape. The tines are light and springy — they glide over grass without tearing it. Perfect for sweeping up leaves.

Garden rake (bow rake): Heavier and sturdier. Has a smaller number of short, thick, rigid metal tines. Built for breaking up hard soil, leveling a gravel path, or spreading mulch. It would damage a lawn if dragged across it, but it's excellent for heavy ground work.

In everyday speech, when someone says "I need to get the rake out," they almost always mean the leaf rake. That's the most commonly recognized use.

This is a literary and social-historical meaning, strongly associated with 17th- and 18th-century European society — though you'll still encounter it today in historical fiction, period dramas, and literary discussion.

A rake in this sense is a man — typically wealthy, charming, well-born, and attractive — who lives a life of pleasure, self-indulgence, and moral recklessness. He is not a villain in a cartoonish sense. He is dangerous precisely because he is appealing.

Specifically, a rake in this sense:

  • Seduces women repeatedly and without honorable intention. He is charming and may seem romantic in the moment, but he has no real commitment or loyalty in mind. He treats romantic conquest as a game.
  • Gambles freely and recklessly, treating money as fuel for pleasure rather than something to preserve.
  • Drinks heavily and keeps reckless hours, living without the discipline that respectable society expected of a gentleman.
  • Ignores moral and social rules with confidence — not out of ignorance, but by deliberate, almost gleeful choice.
  • Gets away with it, because his charm, wit, and social standing give him a pass that no ordinary person would receive.

The key distinction between a rake and just a "bad man" is this: the rake is seductive and fascinating. He is the kind of person who walks into a room and becomes the most compelling presence in it. This is what makes him a rake rather than just a scoundrel. The harm he causes is wrapped in glamour.

You'll find this character type in:

  • 18th-century English literature — Lovelace in Samuel Richardson's Clarissa is perhaps the most famous literary rake: brilliant, cultured, and utterly ruthless. Lord Byron in real life had strong rakish qualities.
  • Restoration comedies (English plays from the 1660s–1700s) — The charming, morally loose rake hero was practically a beloved stock character.
  • Modern historical romance — In the Bridgerton series, several male leads are described as rakes or having a "rakish reputation."

Today, calling someone a rake is somewhat old-fashioned — you wouldn't use it in a casual text. But it survives in literary discussion, historical conversation, and occasionally in the amused phrase "a bit of a rake," used with a knowing tone about someone with a colorful romantic history.

The adjective from this meaning is rakish — it means having the qualities of a rake, or more loosely, looking dashingly and carelessly stylish. A hat worn at a slight angle, for instance, might be described as sitting rakishly on someone's head.

In engineering, architecture, theater, naval design, and several craft fields, rake refers to the angle of deliberate inclination — the degree to which something leans or slopes away from perfectly vertical or perfectly horizontal.

If a structure is designed to tilt or slope at an angle, that tilt is its rake.

This is easiest to understand through specific examples:

On a theater stage:

A raked stage is a stage floor that slopes downward from the back toward the audience — higher at the back (called "upstage") and lower at the front (called "downstage"). This design means audience members seated at the back of a flat-floored theater can still see the actors clearly, including their feet, without the front rows blocking the view.

The angle of this slope is "the rake." A stage manager might say, "Watch your footing — the rake is quite steep," warning actors they're working on a noticeably sloped floor.

This is also where the theater terms "upstage" and "downstage" come from. On old raked stages, moving toward the back of the stage literally meant moving to a higher elevation — moving up. Moving toward the audience was moving down.

On a ship:

The rake of a mast is how far the mast leans backward (toward the back of the ship) rather than standing perfectly upright. Traditionally, a slight backward lean was considered elegant and gave a ship a sleek, fast-looking silhouette.

The rake of the bow (front of the ship) or the stern (back of the ship) describes how much those sections of the hull angle outward over the water, rather than dropping straight down.

On a motorcycle:

The rake angle is the angle of the front suspension fork measured from a vertical line. This directly determines how the bike handles.

  • A large rake (front wheel pushed far forward, fork leaning far back) gives a long, low, relaxed look — the classic chopper or cruiser motorcycle. Such bikes feel very stable at highway speeds but are slow to steer.
  • A small rake (fork nearly upright) makes a nimble, responsive bike — like a sport or racing motorcycle.

This is a major design choice. The difference in feel between a Harley-Davidson and a sport bike is substantially because of differences in rake angle.

On a roof:

In construction, the rake of a gabled (triangular-ended) roof is the sloping edge that runs from the peak (ridge) down to the corner at each triangular end. This diagonal edge is covered by a rake board or rake trim — a piece of material that finishes and protects that edge from rain and weather.

In woodworking and tool design:

The rake angle of a cutting tool — a saw blade, a chisel, a plane — is the angle of the cutting edge relative to the surface being cut. A steeper rake cuts more aggressively and quickly; a shallower one cuts more slowly but more smoothly and cleanly. Skilled craftspeople choose tools with specific rake angles depending on the material and the quality of finish they want.

The common thread in all technical uses: Rake always refers to a deliberate, designed inclination — not a flaw or accident, but a calculated feature that affects how something performs or looks.
4. The Casino's Cut from a Gambling Pot

In gambling — particularly poker — the rake is the fee or commission that the casino or card room takes from each hand played.

Here's the context: in games like blackjack or roulette, the casino plays against you and earns money when you lose. But in poker, players compete against each other, not against the house. The casino simply provides the table, the dealer, the chips, and the space. In return for this service, it takes a small percentage of each pot. That percentage is the rake.

Example: A poker hand ends. The pot is ₹10,000. The rake is 5%. The dealer removes ₹500 from the pot before handing the rest to the winner. The winner receives ₹9,500. The casino keeps ₹500.

The rake is how casinos make money from poker despite not being a player in the game.

In online poker, the software automatically deducts the rake before awarding the pot.

Many games have a rake cap — a maximum limit on how much the house can take, regardless of the pot size. For example: "5% rake, capped at ₹500" means that even if the pot is ₹50,000, the casino only takes ₹500.

In looser, everyday speech, people sometimes use "rake" or "rake-off" to mean any unofficial commission or cut that a middleman takes — often with the slight implication that it's a little shady. "He gets a rake-off from every deal that passes through him."
One Additional (British English) Usage Worth Knowing

In British English, particularly in railway culture, a rake can refer to a set of railway coaches or wagons coupled together to form a train. "A rake of coaches" means a sequence of passenger carriages joined end-to-end. This usage is common among railway enthusiasts and professionals in the UK, but rare elsewhere.

Here is every meaning of rake as a noun:

1. The garden tool — A long-handled tined tool for gathering leaves, leveling soil, and clearing yard debris. Comes in a light leaf-rake version and a heavy garden-rake version.

2. The dissolute man — A charming, wealthy, morally reckless man who pursues pleasure — especially seduction — without restraint or scruple. A figure from literature, history, and period drama.

3. An angle or slope — The deliberate inclination of a structure from vertical or horizontal. Used in theater (stage slope), shipbuilding (mast and hull lean), motorcycles (fork angle), roofing (sloping edge), and woodworking (blade angle).

4. The casino's cut — The percentage fee a poker room or casino takes from each gambling pot as its revenue for hosting the game.
